title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and the justice system

draft.title: Indigenous peoples and the justice system
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are imprisoned at far higher rates than other Australians. They are also a much larger share of prisoners than of the general population.
The Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody (1987 to 1991) examined why so many Aboriginal people died in custody. Its 1991 report made 339 recommendations.

The Royal Commission found that the main cause was not worse treatment inside prisons. It was that Aboriginal people were over-represented in custody in the first place, linked to disadvantage and past policies.

Later reviews, such as the Australian Law Reform Commission's Pathways to Justice report (2017), looked again at the high rates. They urged measures such as diversion from custody and community-led programs.
draft.remember: High imprisonment rates led to inquiries that looked at the causes, not only at conditions in custody.

a.q: What did the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody find about why so many Aboriginal people died in custody?
opts: Aboriginal people were over-represented in custody
Aboriginal people were treated worse than others in cells
Aboriginal people were more often found guilty of murder
Aboriginal people were held longer than the law allowed
a.why: The Royal Commission found that the deaths were linked to the number of Aboriginal people taken into custody, tied to disadvantage and past policies. Treatment inside cells is the tempting option, but the Commission did not find it to be the main cause.
a.clue: Think about how people came to be in custody at all.

b.q: A review in a state finds that Aboriginal people make up a small share of the population but a large share of its prisoners. Which response best matches the approach of the later reviews and inquiries?
opts: Divert people from custody and fund community-led programs
Build more prisons so that cells are less crowded
Treat the gap as a problem inside prisons only
Wait for the rates to fall as the population grows
b.why: The ALRC's Pathways to Justice report urged diversion from custody and community-led programs, which target the causes of high imprisonment. Focusing only on prison conditions is tempting, but the inquiries looked at why people end up in custody.
b.clue: The inquiries looked at why people end up in custody.

a.best: Aboriginal people were over-represented in custody

b.best: Divert people from custody and fund community-led programs

problems.detail: The remember line says high imprisonment rates led to the inquiries. The card says the Royal Commission was set up to examine why so many Aboriginal people died in custody, so its trigger was deaths in custody, not imprisonment rates. This adds a causal claim the card does not make.
The clue ('Think about how people came to be in custody at all') points straight at the over-representation option, so a student could answer without knowing the finding.

check.summary: The facts check out: RCIADIC ran from 1987 to 1991 with 339 recommendations, it found the main cause was over-representation, and the ALRC's Pathways to Justice report was 2017. Two minor flags: the remember line implies imprisonment rates triggered the Royal Commission rather than deaths in custody, and question a's clue nearly gives the answer away.
